name: Bitumen of Judea

card.summary: A natural Dead Sea asphalt used since antiquity, associated in folk lore with mumia and shilajit and in modern times known for its role in early photography.
card.note: A natural asphalt; no tested cosmetic use.

quick.overview:
Bitumen of Judea is a natural asphalt from the Dead Sea region, long used as an adhesive, waterproofing material and in embalming. In appearance discussion it appears as a relative of mumia and shilajit, the mineral pitches that some traditions have credited with healing and rejuvenation.

Its best-documented use is photographic: Nicéphore Niépce coated a pewter plate with it in the 1820s to make the oldest surviving camera photograph. No published human study tests it for skin or looks.
quick.how: In its documented uses it is dissolved in solvents such as turpentine and applied as a coating or resist, or used as a wood stain; it is not a standard cosmetic.
quick.risks: No cosmetic safety data exist. It is a hydrocarbon material, and heating gives off a sulfur odour.

lead: Bitumen of Judea is a naturally occurring asphalt linked to the Dead Sea. It has been used since antiquity as a wood colourant and, from the 1820s, as a light-sensitive coating in photography.[1]

Nicéphore Niépce coated a pewter plate with it in 1826 or 1827 and photographed the view from his estate, which is usually described as the oldest surviving camera photograph; light hardened the bitumen and a solvent washed away the rest.[1][2]
It is mentioned alongside mumia and shilajit as a pitch in traditional medicine and embalming; no appearance use has been studied.

angle.text: It appears in appearance contexts only through its association with mumia and shilajit. Documented uses are in art, printmaking and photography.

paras: It is a dark, viscous to solid material that dissolves in turpentine and some other terpenes and can be mixed with oils, waxes and varnishes.[1][2]

Antique uses included adhesive and sealant roles and embalming according to a descriptive encyclopedia source.[2] In the nineteenth century it served as a photoresist for printing plates, coated, exposed, developed with solvent and acid-etched.[1]

timeline.event: Niépce makes the earliest surviving camera photograph using bitumen of Judea (sometimes dated 1827).[1]
